entries.title: The Best Black Horror Books, recommended by Maurice Broaddus
entries.summary: Black horror books and films have been making waves in recent years, from the blockbuster success of Jordan Peele's Get Out to Victor LaValle's multi-award-winning novella The Ballad of Black Tom. We asked Maurice Broaddus – author, librarian and editor of a new, canonical Black horror anthology – to recommend five unmissable books featuring horror stories by Black writers. This interview appeared
entries.content:
Let me just begin by asking: Is it a good time for Black horror writing?

It’s a great time for Black horror writing. In the recent past, Black horror has just sort of permeated the pop culture consciousness. When the movie Get Out was released, it put Black horror right into the mainstream. You also have movies like Sinners suddenly dominating the cinema.

So you have all that going on, and on top of that, there is this resurgence of Black horror in genre writing—you have The Ballad of Black Tom, you have Ring Shout, you have Let’s Play White, all these different books reestablishing the literary canon that is Black horror.

Black horror especially seems to surface when we are living in more oppressive times. They are stories of resilience and resistance, of acting through one’s agency, and of how to navigate terrifying times.

If you look historically, you’ll see that this sort of writing has always bubbled right there beneath the surface, going back to Pauline Hopkins in the mid 19th century, all the way through stories written through the Jim Crow era. There have always been stories that have positioned us as fighting against the systems we live under.

Were you seeking to highlight this history in your anthology, Black Horror: Canonical Voices from Then to Now? You worked with Dr Chesya Burke to compile this new publication.

It wasn’t so much that as positioning that anthology in conversation with a couple of other anthologies— Sheree Renée Thomas’s Dark Matter, which looks at the length and breadth of history of speculative Black fiction, and Jordan Peele’s Out There Screaming, which asks what the modern scene looks like. We thought, hey, what is the journey between those two points? What does the current Black horror scene look like, and what did the rise of that scene look like? And, through the lens of community: What does that burgeoning Black literary community look like?

I’m going to ask you about each of your book recommendations in turn, starting with Tananarive Due’s The Reformatory, which came out in 2023. It’s set in a reform school in Jim Crow-era Florida. Would you tell us more?

One of the things about Tananarive Due is that she’s sort of the shadow under which we all work, when it comes to the modern Black horror scene. She came to prominence in the 1990s with My Soul to Keep, and she’s the one we still look to. Tananarive Due is out there doing the thing. Tananarive and Octavia Butler; I remember writing my first short story the same year Octavia Butler published Parable of the Sower, so I feel I’ve marked my career by those two women.

With The Reformatory, you see a master storyteller writing in the strength of her full powers. It ties in a sense of real history, pursues powerful characters through the system, and, again, it goes back to those themes I was talking about: What does it look like to resist and survive under that system, those conditions.

I haven’t had a chance to read her latest one, Mazywood, yet.

Speculative fiction seems a very interesting way to wrestle with what are, essentially, haunted histories. Of embodying them in a new, strange way.

Absolutely. I think the power of speculative fiction is that you can have all these powerful conversations, difficult conversations, because there is that bit of a remove. We can put it in an alien context, or put it in a fantasy context, and then it’s easier to have those conversations.

With horror, the context gets more difficult. We don’t put the same remove in there, we make it even more uncomfortable and difficult , and that’s going to be part of that rollercoaster of living through that history all over again.

You’ve already briefly mentioned your next book recommendation, which is The Ballad of Black Tom, which was released in 2016. It’s a reimagining of a H.P. Lovecraft story.

Yes. It’s interesting that Lovecraft has loomed so large over the speculative fiction world, and especially in the horror world. As Black creatives, how are we to position ourselves in the shadow of this huge racist, who basically demonises us?

But then a book like The Ballad of Black Tom says: hey, you know what? Alright. Let’s wrestle with this, let’s reimagine it. You tried to demonise us, so let’s interrogate you through story. So it’s a response to Lovecraft in some ways, but it also asks what the real horror is underneath. Is it the systems we live in, the systems you created? How are we going to survive and thrive? While also dealing with that existential dread that is out there.

It’s described as a ‘fantasy horror novella.’ Novellas seem to be very popular in horror writing—much more so than in other genres.

Novellas are actually my favourite length to write. My absolute favourite. Tor.com were the first to bring back the novella form, around 2015 or 2016. Nnedi Okorafor’s Binti came out around that time too. Before that, novellas were basically a dead market. They weren’t seen as a profitable thing. So I was writing all these stories, without anywhere to publish them, and then all of a sudden they came back into favour.

But the novella used to be a standard. I mean, if you look at a lot of so-called literary classics, many of them are basically novellas. Then they fell out of fashion because publishers believed people wanted more bang for their buck. But we really do like novellas, these quick reads. We can read the entire thing in one sitting, but still feel enmeshed in this world. The Ballad of Black Tom shows exactly what that length can do.

Let’s talk next about Justina Ireland’s Dread Nation, which came out in 2018. It offers an exciting alternate American history, in which the Civil War takes a terrifying turn as zombies rise from their graves at the Battle of Gettysburg.

I don’t think even Justina understands the impact of that book on the rest of the scene. Until then, we just hadn’t seen that sort of work rise up and take the market by storm.

Dread Nation reminds me of that tabletop supernatural role playing game, which dealt with the Weird West—Deadlands. It very much has that Deadlands vibe, where you’re dealing with alternate history, the Civil War, then throw in zombies on top of that. Then through all that, she’s asking questions about race; about wrestling with monsters (dare I say “ghosts”) of the past.

Dread Nation is a really seminal book, and there were a series of books that hit the scene at the same time with alternate takes on history, including Cherie Priest’s Boneshaker. All these genre-mashing books, where they are not one thing but rather meshing two together. Boneshaker was alternate history, but you also had a steampunk vibe. Dread Nation has alternate history and zombies—two great tastes that taste great together. Bringing zombies into alternate history was a powerful injection into the genre at the time; storytelling that hadn’t been done before.

I keep coming back to this thread through a lot of Black horror: the whole idea of revisiting history in new and fresh ways. With Dread Nation you have that, and I hadn’t seen anything like it since Steven Barnes’ Lion’s Blood, an alternate history of the slave trade. As with Dread Nation, you have that sense of turning history on its head, and bringing a sense of horror all at the same time.

Right, and there’s further meshing of genres in An Unkindness of Ghosts by Rivers Solomon.

It has the same vibes going through it. Basically, you have this Southern plantation system reimagined on a generational starship. So, as a reader, you’re like: What just happened?

You have the main character who—these themes touch a little close to home—has been approved by the system, so she gets to navigate through the system in a sort of enlightened role. But on another level, how does she relate to her friends and family still caught up in the rest of the system? She’s navigating both worlds, to the point where she has to choose.

An Unkindness of Ghosts has one of my favourite deathbed scenes of all time. I don’t want to say too much, but one of the main characters, a close friend, is dying, and gives a terrific speech railing against the system and the world and the protagonist needing to choose her place in it. I remember reading the scene and throwing the book aside thinking, yeah, that’s the speech I want to hear.

What does she gain by setting this in space?

I’m in two minds about it. On one hand: in the far-flung future, we’re in generational starships, yet we are still wrestling with this antebellum type system. So I feel like – oh man – a certain way about that. But on the other hand, it lets us look at this system in a whole new way. Because we don’t have the trappings of the antebellum South, the whole story is recontextualised, and we can have different nuanced conversations because of that. And we’re not trading on torture porn, oppression porn, or anything like that. We can examine issues of oppression through this new lens.

So it’s a delicate tightrope that Rivers is walking with this story, but it does allow us to enmesh ourselves in the story without the whole weight of history behind it. Because enslavement was a horrific time, and it’s hard to mine that for entertainment, frankly. Recontextualising it allows us to have the room to brief and examine the issues with a bit of remove.

That brings us to your final book recommendation, which you mentioned right at the start: Jordan Peele’s anthology Out There Screaming: An Anthology of New Black Horror. Why do you recommend it?

If you want a nice sample platter of Black horror, you won’t get a much better book that this. I mean, yes, I have a story in this book, one of my favourite stories I’ve written, but you also have most of the heavy hitters in this genre, and some of the great up-and-coming writers. So if you like short stories and you want a sense of the breadth of the genre, this is a great one-stop-shop.

That feels like something you’ve aimed to get across in this interview—the true range of writing out there.

Yes, absolutely. Take An Unkindness of Ghosts, it’s a sci-fi horror novel. The Ballad of Black Tom is Black horror but it’s also cosmic horror because it’s dealing with H.P. Lovecraft. With The Reformatory, we have historical horror. With Dread Nation, you have traditional monsters and this alt-history element.

So you see all this genre-blending under the umbrella of horror. And in Jordan Peele’s anthology, you have a lot of atmospheric horror, a lot of psychological horror, and all together a broad tour of what the Black horror scene looks like today.

Is there anything else you’d like to mention?

I should say that, for the most part, we’re actually looking at horror through a Black American lens. So we’re not taking into account stories of the rest of the diaspora: What does Caribbean horror look like? What does African horror look like? I do need to do a deeper dive into these other areas, to see how they are interrogating this idea of what horror looks like.

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor

November 17, 2026. Updated: November 19, 2026

entries.title: The Best French Short Stories, recommended by Patrick McGuinness
entries.summary: The French short story tradition is varied and innovative. Patrick McGuinness, editor of the Penguin collections, introduces five of the best, all of which "understand that the short story can be anything it wants, but it does actually have to be short." Ranging in content from the fantastic to the achingly banal, these gems of the genre will leave you pondering them for much longer than they took
entries.content:
The French short story tradition is varied and innovative. Patrick McGuinness, editor of the Penguin collections, introduces five of the best, all of which "understand that the short story can be anything it wants, but it does actually have to be short." Ranging in content from the fantastic to the achingly banal, these gems of the genre will leave you pondering them for much longer than they took to read.

I won’t ask you for a definition of short stories, as you write in your anthology that “it is easier – as well as more enjoyable – to read short stories than to define them.” So could we instead introduce people to the range and variety of the French short story tradition?

Yes. When I was putting the anthology together, I was trying to work out what counted as a short story. The French like categorising things. They like things to have borders, pigeonholes, and definitions, and once they’ve got them, they like blurring the borders and exploding the categories and smudging the definitions. I think that’s a pretty good way to proceed. So my question to myself as I began was, where does one start?

When you think about the French short story, you think of the classic 19th-century short story, with a beginning, middle, and an end – not necessarily in that order. These have a shape and, if not a formula, at least some traits by which they can be recognised as a short story. But you don’t necessarily know where you’re going to stop with these kinds of definitions… Some of the stories that I chose were pieces of memoir that were framed as stories. Others were pieces of newspaper headline – if you think about it, a small ad in a newspaper is a story, isn’t it? A lot of the writers I was interested in were playing with the form, asking what it was and what it could do.

All the stories today appear in your anthologies, although some are also available in their original collections. Tell us about the anthologies’ scope.

My anthology starts with the late medieval period and goes on through to the world of a few years ago, the 2020s. They all understand that the short story can be anything it wants, but it does actually have to be short. It doesn’t have to be a story. But it has to be short, and it needs to go in, do its job, and then go away again. And I hope that that’s what I have found in these different examples.

As with a lot of these anthologies, the word ‘French’ is less solid than it looks. Quite a lot of the people I put in are coming from different parts of the world. The ‘Frenchness’ of these writers was something I was interested in pushing and exploring, and that’s why there’s a lot of Swiss and Belgian and North African, all sorts of francophone writing.

Great. Well, let’s begin with the very short, published in 1906: Felix Fénéon’s Three Line Novellas (also translated as Novels in Three Lines)

In French, it’s Nouvelles en Trois Lignes. This takes us to the various definitions that the French have – there’s the conte, which is like a traditional story; the recit, which is often defined as a story, and a way of telling a story, that foregrounds its own telling and its own narrator; and the nouvelle. ‘Nouvelle’ doesn’t map directly onto ‘novella’– it’s often much shorter, but that’s how it’s often translated.

Fénéon was a very brilliant art critic, and he was very mischievous. He was one of those writers who thought that everyday life contained as much drama and sorrow and tragedy and comedy and – importantly – absurdity, as all of the best put-together short stories. So he creates these tales which are true – he gleans them from what the French would have called the petite brèves, the day-to-day little news morsels, a sort of news in brief.

I find them very sardonic, very funny, and very sad. I think that with these stories, Fénéon is trying to make reality speak for itself in as unmediated a way as possible, while also making his readers sense the spectacular nature of everyday life.

You talk in your foreword about using the length as a resource rather than just a limit, which I thought was a lovely way of looking at it – can we talk a bit about that?

That’s right. With these tiny micro stories – I guess they are the forerunners of what we would call microfiction (although they’re micro facts.) – the length is a resource. You cannot successfully do anything in any form, whatever it is – whether it’s an eight-hundred-page novel, a sonnet, or whatever – unless you respect the demands of its size, shape, and so on. And once you do that, you realise that the shortness is a resource… The distinction between form and content is something that we’re taught in school. But doing things properly, form and content should be inseparable (when you’re writing – perhaps when you’re analysing, you take them apart).

With the three-line novellas, Fénéon is showing you that even in three lines, you can have tone and style. There’s no form, no length too short for personality to express itself.

Your second choice oozes personality. Please introduce Huysmans’s “M. Bougran’s Retirement.”

Joris-Karl Huysmans wrote a very famous novel called À Rebours, translated as Against Nature, which is the book Dorian Gray reads in The Picture of Dorian Gray, and it influences his decadent immorality and so on. The novel was a huge intervention in the culture: it was described as falling like a meteorite into the literary landscape. It’s the story of a hopelessly snobby, very rich aristocrat who escapes from the world, decorates his palace in exactly the way he wants, and has a tortoise encrusted with jewels and so on.

One of the things that Huysmans was fundamentally interested in was escape and the failure to escape. “M. Bougran’s Retirement” seems to me a rather sad and funny and caustic short story about a man who can’t bear to retire. When he finally does accept that he has to retire, he goes back to his crappy little flat and has it decorated exactly like his office, and gets a big desk, and even pays a local boy to bring him bits of paper that he can stamp. I find that incredibly sad, incredibly poignant.

When I was younger, I found it hilarious, and as I inch towards retirement myself, I start to find it actually too close for comfort. I think there’s something there about work, about how work bleeds us dry, but also how we are ready to be bled. It’s a bleak but very funny story – and the sort of story which a reader could read two or three times and find it completely different each time, depending on how they were feeling.

I found it horribly relatable, and I’m not retiring, just trying to make myself stop at weekends. It was rejected at first for being so unlike the novel that he was loved for. Was he going off in a new direction generally at this point, or is he using the short story as a chance to experiment?

Quite a lot of his novels had been about people trying and failing to escape, and he tries various means… The question of escape in Huysmans’s work is everywhere. Later on in his life, he became a devout Catholic, and he didn’t renege in any way on what he’d written before, but the books become much more about an escape into religion. So they’ve all got that one thing in common.

People didn’t like “M. Bougran’s Retirement” because they felt that he wasn’t doing what they wanted him to do, and yet in a strange way they recognised his major themes and preoccupations. They just weren’t delivered in the same way, or not in the right way. They were made sad and ridiculous, poor and threadbare.

Bring back the jewel-encrusted tortoises.

That’s right. If you’re going to play this game, play it with a lot of money and lots of luxuries.

Let’s talk about your third choice – a very literal escape artist in this one. Tell us about Marcel Aymé’s The Man Who Walked Through Walls.

This is a story that I’ve loved since I first read it as a child, because it has these magical properties delivered – like a lot of Marcel Aymé’s surrealism – in a deadpan style. What’s ‘the man who walked through walls’ going to do with his extraordinary gift? Not very much, actually. Likewise, the beautiful beginning, the accidental nature of how he discovers his gift…

It was a much-loved, very successful story. People felt in some strange way they could relate to it, because the marvellous becomes banal, but also the banal can become marvellous. There’s this strange Mobius strip you get in Aymé’s work where fantasy and a flat reality don’t seem to oppose each other anymore. They become each other’s avenues – one gives rise to the other and falls back into the other.

In a strange way, Marcel Aymé and the Huysmans are both about ordinariness: what is the ordinary? Is it formed by habit? Do we get used to the extraordinary to the point where it becomes ordinary, or is it a quality in itself? Is it a thing that we make through constant exposure to it? Marcel Aymé tried a few other variants on that, but nothing was ever as popular as The Man Who Could Walk Through Walls. Le Passe-muraille, it’s called in French, which is even more beautiful – ‘The Wall-Crosser,’ literally translated.

The fantastic has a big role in the French short story tradition. Could we talk a little about that? Is this story representative?

Yes, one of the big feeders of the French short story in the mid-to-late 19th century was the ‘fantastique’. Many writers had a go at doing a version of it, and it very quickly became something tricksy and often amusing, and also in its own way very conventional. There are rules in the fantastic: it isn’t the same as the surreal. The fantastic needs to be logical; the fantastic things that happen need to be believable within their fantastical universe.

It was also a reaction against the 19th century’s increasing secularism and belief in rationality. What’s the first thing you do when you have converted everything mystical into rationality? You want some more mysticism, don’t you? No one ever sits there and says, ‘Great, everything’s really rational now. We can rest.’ I always remember being excited as a teenager when I discovered that Arthur Conan Doyle — author of Sherlock Holmes, the most rational detective, the answerer of questions par excellence – Arthur Conan Doyle himself was a big believer in ghosts and fairies and the occult and all of that. Is that cognitive dissonance? No, I don’t think it is. I think it’s some strange need to balance: the impulse for the inexplicable never goes away. So when you’ve explained loads of things, you start finding things you can’t explain. Flaubert has a version of that where he says that knowledge is a circle, and as the circle of knowledge expands, so does the circumference of the circle that touches on ignorance.

Marcel Aymé’s story is a reply, perhaps, or an attempt to recharge the late 19th-century fantastic heritage, but then to apply it in a rather grey, middle-of-the-road Paris – austerity Paris.

Could you tell us about your fourth choice? Next we have “Revelation” by Marie Ndiaye.

This is a very moving, rather sad story about betrayal, and feelings never quite coming off – or not having the right feelings for the right people. It’s visceral, because it’s a mother and child. I liked its unresolvedness and its epiphanic non-epiphany – because the idea that we must always learn something is another thing that stories play with, of course. Some of my favourite books, especially of the 19th century – like Flaubert’s Sentimental Education, or Musil’s Man Without Qualities – they’re framed as novels about self-education, the bildungsroman. But what happens if you learn nothing? It’s left to the reader to learn something or to feel something.

It feels extremely contemporary, and very French. It’s also about alienation and discomfort. It happens on a bus, so there’s a sense of the stages of the journey being staging posts of feeling and of narrative. I generally like films and stories that have the shape of a journey, especially a journey that doesn’t go anywhere.

In sum, what would you say it’s about? It’s a hard one to describe without telling the whole story, as it’s sparse…

Yes. It’s about… someone who betrays their child by not feeling for them.

Ah, perfect.

It’s about betrayal and self-justification and the failure of self-justification. We might also think of that classic French idea of bad faith, where we lie to ourselves, and we know we are lying to ourselves, but we choose to pretend to ourselves that we believe the lie in order to get or do what we want. I was very struck by the way this story beautifully and poignantly finds the staging posts of that emotional drama.

We’ve come now – alas, another poignant staging post – to your last choice. This is “The Disappearance of Honoré Subrac” by Apollinaire…

I was very pleased to find this for the anthology because Apollinaire didn’t do many short stories. This one is playing with the fantastic genre, but it also has a certain element of ridiculousness and comedy and burlesque, almost music hall stuff – adultery and wardrobes and beds and things like that. But it is a very revealing story as well, because it is nonetheless about emotions, and in some strange way about honour. I thought it had huge amounts of personality.

A bit like The Man Who Walked Through Walls, it’s about what one does with special powers and gifts. This one seemed to me to be more melodramatic, perhaps more comical as well. Like a lot of these stories as well, the framing device is a narrator telling you something in a slightly tongue-in-cheek way, and the framing here works quite nicely.

He does so much work in those first couple of paragraphs. It boils down to ‘No one can solve this disappearance, and I told them the truth but no one believes me, which is fair enough’ – which opens up a world of expectation.

Yes – and actually that reminds me that quite a lot of those stories in the fantastic genre are framed in such a way that the reader is being told a secret, which they will then keep or know or believe as well. They’re involving in that way. ‘I’m telling you, reader, this: no one believes me, but you will.’ I think that’s why people like the fantastique too – they’ve got a stake in it. When cleverly and correctly handled, it’s one of these genres that draws people in, and you can’t fluff it because you don’t have much time.

Patrick McGuinness is a British-Belgian writer and academic. The author of two novels, a memoir and two books of poems, he teaches French and Comparative Literature at Oxford, where he is a Fellow of St Anne's College.

entries.title: The best books on The Panama Canal, recommended by Julie Greene
entries.summary: The Panama Canal was an engineering feat but also a social feat, coordinating tens of thousands of workers, uprooting their families, and displacing a former world in the heart of Panama. Historian Julie Greene picks five books to tell the story of the Panama Canal from every angle - from the early attempts to the economic outcomes, via the extraordinary lives of the men and women who made it poss
entries.content:
The Panama Canal was an engineering feat but also a social feat, coordinating tens of thousands of workers, uprooting their families, and displacing a former world in the heart of Panama. Historian Julie Greene picks five books to tell the story of the Panama Canal from every angle - from the early attempts to the economic outcomes, via the extraordinary lives of the men and women who made it possible.

Let’s begin at the beginning: why was the Panama Canal built?

The idea of building a canal across the Isthmus of Panama had been a dream for centuries. Traffic otherwise had to go around the southern tip of South America, which made the trip thousands of miles longer.

The first step was a railroad built in the 1850s, the first transcontinental railroad in the Western Hemisphere. Then the French tried and failed, tragically and infamously. Then the US tried. The US, in addition to wanting to avoid that long trip, saw it as useful for a range of economic and military reasons. It was sparked by the so-called Spanish-American War, during which it took a long time for the US Navy to travel around that southern tip.

It was also a time when Theodore Roosevelt, as president, had great ambitions for the US. He wanted the US to become a global power commensurate with Europe, and saw military and naval power in particular as key to that.

High stakes. On to your first choice: tell us about The Path Between the Seas, by David McCullough.

This is still by far the most widely read book about the Canal’s history, and it has a lot of strengths. It won several prizes for good reason. McCullough is a wonderful writer, and he brings forward a sweeping pageant of life. It has a broad chronology: it covers both the French and the US construction efforts. So, there’s good reason why it’s still so widely read today.

It is, by the standards of the other books I’ll talk about, rather triumphalist in the way it sees US power in the Canal Zone, and the importance of the Canal. Theodore Roosevelt would read the book and think it beautifully expressed his view: that this was not about imperialism, but was a gift to global civilization based on American strength in medicine, engineering, technology, etc.

It’s definitely a great book to read. Many people who are taking a cruise through the Canal think of it first, and it’s a great contrast to the other books that we’ll talk about.

As I understand it from your own book, a triumphalist narrative was not unanimously shared at the time it was being built…

Yes – and McCullough covers that. He has a wonderful eye for the ironies of history. So when I say it’s triumphalist, I don’t mean that he completely erases the downsides. He certainly discusses the ways in which it was a pretty naked grab by the United States, for example…

Tell us more.

The United States wanted the Canal and tried to negotiate with Colombia – Panama at that time was a part of Colombia. Colombia refused, so the United States let it be known among Panamanians that the US would support a revolt, and sent warships. Then when the revolt happened, the US immediately negotiated a treaty that gave it permanent and complete control, “as if it were sovereign”, over the Panama Canal Zone. So this young country, at its birth, had the entire heart of its country taken away from it.

Let’s start digging into these contrasting stories. Your second choice is Dying to Better Themselves, by Olive Senior. Could you introduce us?

Olive Senior is Jamaican, best known for her poetry and novels, so she came to this task—a nonfiction book focused on Caribbean workers—with these incredible writing skills. So first of all, it’s just a really beautiful narrative. She integrates cultural sources like songs and fictional writings into how she understands the Caribbean people.

She centres the Caribbean itself in this story: she shows how the building of the Canal, and the vast migrations across the Caribbean that made it possible, reshaped not only Panama but the Caribbean too. In addition, like McCullough, she covers a broader chronology. She begins with Caribbean migration during the construction of the railroad in the 1850s, goes through the French Canal project, and then through the US project; so it gives us a longer context for understanding the relationship between the Caribbean and the Canal. And finally, she moves the chronology forward as well, following what happened when the Canal was finished: migration back home or permanent settlement in Panama.

Throughout all of that, she takes this group – the Caribbean, mostly male labour force that we think we know – and she shows us the complexity of it: the ways they accommodated themselves to the power of the United States and to life in Panama or the Zone, and the ways they resisted. It’s a beautiful book that marked new approaches to thinking about the history of the Canal.

It’s maybe worth underscoring here what a huge part of the workforce we’re referring to – I believe you wrote that over 30,000 out of the 62,000-strong population of the Zone were from the Caribbean. Could we talk about this link? The US was actively recruiting there, right?

Right. They went to the Caribbean because people there were English speaking, and they were thought to be more easily disciplined. They tended not to use the local workers, so there were relatively few Panamanians, only a few thousand.

The workforce was very hierarchical. There was the so-called ‘unskilled labour’, which was Caribbean workers; and then ‘skilled labour’ was predominantly white US workers, and a few thousand Europeans as well. For a while, they brought in Spaniards and Italians and Greeks, thinking they might help push the Caribbean workers to work harder.

Your next choice takes us to a more hidden world of labour: tell us about Joan Flores-Villalobos’s The Silver Women: How Black Women’s Labour Made The Panama Canal.

Yes, as you say, this takes us to the work and the world of Caribbean women. Much of the work that’s been done by McCullough, and even by Senior, has tended to give less attention to women. The sources are harder to find on the Caribbean women; it’s much more of a hidden world. Joanne Flores Villalobos had to tease out the information from creative use of sources.

She also came to it wanting to understand different things. She framed the book as focused on social reproduction, the work that women did to make it possible for the work on the Canal to happen: the work of feeding, caring for the sick, housing… All of that work becomes important in her story.

Along the way, she shows that understanding women more fully changes our entire understanding of the project. They shaped the economy, and like the male labourers, they had to choose between accommodating themselves to the power of the US or resisting – typically, of course, doing some of both. They negotiated wages; they fought for more respect; they went to court over insults issued against them. They fought to get money from husbands or domestic partners who abandoned them. One of the most common jobs they had was in the home of a white US housewife, so she also shows us how empire shapes intimate relations by zooming in on how these women interacted with their bosses.

Official policy did not at first encourage women joining, right?

Yes, that is a really interesting part of it. The US thought it would be too messy and complicated to have women there, whether from the US or from the Caribbean. There’s a story that I’ve never been able to find the actual evidence for, that the reason the US relented and started allowing women to come was that the Caribbean workers had a sit-down strike and said, “No women, no work” – and then the white workers did the same thing.

The Canal project started in 1904, and by 1908-9 there were thousands of women there – both white housewives from the US, and Caribbean women who came for much the same reasons as their menfolk did. They came sometimes to support their men and make sure they had someone who would cook for them, but also to escape the hardships of their home islands, Jamaica or Barbados. And sometimes because they wanted some adventure, and thought they could make more money building the Yankees’ Canal.

Could we quickly explain the title, ‘The Silver Women’ – I assume a reference to the silver and gold system?

Yes. Really crucial to the whole Canal project was the silver and gold system, which was a biracial system in which white workers were paid in gold and other workers, mostly Caribbean, in silver. It’s in many ways comparable to Jim Crow in the United States. It was not just different kinds of currency: the gold workers were treated much better. They had six weeks’ vacation, and they made more money than they would in the US. The silver workers lived in shacks that lacked screens, were much more susceptible to disease and accidents, and were paid much less. In talking about the ‘silver women’, Flores is broadening out from just the currency system, since the majority of these women weren’t actually part of the silver-gold system. She’s looking at the broader significance of the segregation system, and how women responded to it.

All of this circles something fascinating about the Canal: that it didn’t just require engineering feats, but also the creation of a whole autonomous district with tens of thousands of people, which had to be built up in ten years, governed, and then dismantled again. That world is presented in amazing detail in your own book The Canal Builders: could you introduce your project there?

I came to the topic as a labour historian, interested also in issues of race and gender and migration. All of these were things that McCullough dealt with relatively little. I wanted to show that the labour problem in the Canal was really at the heart of the project. We often think of it as a triumph of engineering and medicine, and certainly, that’s how McCullough saw it. But, from the beginning, I took some wisdom from the chief engineer of the project, George Washington Goethals. He said that those aspects really weren’t that innovative. What was innovative was figuring out how to discipline and manage this vast workforce of people – so that’s what The Canal Builders took on.

The book is incredibly rich in personal stories. Could we talk a little about the archives you used?

Yes – the sources are phenomenal, especially from the perspective of it being a United States project. The best place for information about it is the records of the US government held at the National Archives. The government obsessively recorded every single detail. Beyond that, there are records in Panama that helped me understand the project from a Panamanian perspective, and there are records in the United Kingdom, because the Caribbean labourers were colonial subjects of the British Empire, and the British were keeping an eye on them. They would often write to their diplomatic representatives in the UK, and those letters were some of the very best sources I found in terms of the Caribbean experience and perspective.

When I began the project, I thought I was just going to focus on the white skilled workers who went to the canal, and I figured McCullough’s book had probably done it all. But the minute I got into the sources, I saw that the things that interested me were such a small part of his book: how people lived, how people worked, what forms of exploitation they experienced, and how they responded to or reacted against them. There were voluminous sources that brought that part of the story to life. In my very first visit to the National Archives, I realised that there was a book here, the sort of book that I would want to write.

Then I knew I had to go to Panama and see what was there. And a friend of mine who had done work at Kew, at the UK’s National Archives, said, ‘I think no historian working on the Canal has ever visited that archive, but I think you’ll find a lot there…’ So towards the end of my research, I took the plunge and went, and it was a final gold mine.

I loved the details from the letters to consuls. The court records were astonishing too…

Yes. No one had ever looked at those, and I remember searching and searching for where they might be, and it turned out they were here in D.C. at the National Archives. They were incredible – the criminal suits and the prison labour issues, but also the civil records. For example, one of the best ways I traced women’s experiences was looking at the divorce records. The white US men would ask their wives to come join them in Panama – some working-class carpenter’s wife in Detroit, or something – and a lot of wives would say, ‘Hell no, I’m not going to the wilderness that is Panama.’ And then the men would divorce them on grounds of abandonment, because at that time the law said that if you don’t go where your husband wants you to go, you’ve abandoned him. So they divorced their wives, and married some young Panamanian woman, and both the wife and husband would enter letters between them as evidence, going back sometimes years and years. That let me document these marriages, and the lives of working-class men and women. It was really fascinating – a whole world I had no idea about.

Really interesting. Ok, your fourth choice is going to carry the story on beyond the building years: this is Noel Maurer and Carlos Yu’s The Big Ditch: How America Took, Built, Ran, and Ultimately Gave Away the Panama Canal.

I include this book partly because it’s just so different from the others. It’s a little more dry – it’s an economic history of the canal, where the other books we’re talking about lean more towards social history. Maurer and Yu quantitatively and qualitatively examine the economic impact of an imperial project like the Panama Canal. Did it make money? Who did it make money for? How did that change over time?

What they found was really interesting. At first, the Canal’s advantages could be seen pretty clearly. It obviously made traffic cheaper; it saved thousands of miles, etc. But they found that while those improvements helped the global economy, they didn’t really benefit the United States government itself. Furthermore, what they found is that the economic benefits of the Canal had really diminished by the 1960s. So the decision by the US to transfer the Canal to Panama wasn’t some benevolent generosity. It was more that the United States, at this point, really wasn’t finding it that useful. And in that post-colonial period of history, it was unseemly that the US owned the heart of another country. So there were a lot of straightforward reasons.

Was aviation the big factor in the decline, or a change in key trade routes, or…?

Aviation, the interstate highway, and the fact that rail freight became cheaper as diesel was available… Also, the West Coast of the US developed more, and there were more markets there. So the Canal became a little less important.

One of the things Americans usually don’t realise about the Canal is that when the Panamanians took it over, they ran it better. It makes more money, it’s safer, it’s more efficient. They do a better job in every way, which is hard for Americans to believe because we think we’re the best.

Well, that brings us to your last choice. Let’s talk about the Panamanian view on the Panama Canal. Please introduce us to Erased: The Untold Story Of The Panama Canal.

This is a great book to end with because it has a very different approach. It’s by a Panamanian scholar, Marixa Lasso, and she centres Panama in her story. She emphasises that the Canal wasn’t built on empty land, that it was a thriving society, crucial to the Republic of Panama, which had been densely inhabited, urbanised, very active commercially, and shaped by long histories of transportation and exchange. She looks at the impact of the Canal, and in particular, she focuses on the decision of the United States to depopulate most of the zone.

About 40,000 residents of what became the Canal Zone were expelled. For some of them, this was because the building of Gatun Lake and the dam meant that some areas were flooded and people had to leave, but most of it was not necessary. Most of it was just because the United States wanted to have much more control over the landscape. So it’s about how the imperial power, the United States, produced a whole new landscape. They had to create replacement settlements, and they had segregated communities reorganised along the corridor.

Then, on top of all of that, she’s really interesting for thinking about Panama’s place in the world. For example, she talks about the ways in which the US saw itself as modern and bringing modernity to Panama, and she looks at the ways in which Panama was already modern, and the ways that the United States messed with its sense of itself and its own modernity.

Ultimately – this is perhaps the most important thing – she connects the depopulation and the erasure of communities to erasures of memory, and the ways in which Panama itself is written out of the story of the Panama Canal.

Julie Greene

Julie Greene is a historian of United States, transnational, and global labor and immigration. She is the author of Box 25: Archival Secrets, Caribbean Workers, and the Panama Canal, which explores a set of remarkable memoirs written by canal workers (and held in Box 25 at the Library of Congress) as the starting point for considering migration, power, and silences in history. Previously, Greene authored The Canal Builders: Making America's Empire at the Panama Canal, which received the Organization of American Historians’ James A. Rawley Prize for the best book on the history of race relations.
